title: Eight switches
hook: Each switch is only on or off. How far can eight of them count?

knows: that computers store things as 1s and 0s
doesNotKnow: what a bit or byte holds

misconception: Eight on/off switches can only stand for about eight (or sixteen) numbers, because each switch carries one small piece; binary is a code rather than a way of counting.
objective: The learner can explain that each switch is worth twice the one to its right, so eight switches reach 255 (256 numbers counting 0), and one more switch doubles the count.

claims.text: With switches worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128, all eight on make 255.
Eight switches have 256 different on/off patterns, and each names exactly one whole number from 0 to 255. With all eight on the stage says: with 0, that is 256 numbers.
claims.source: 2^8 = 256 patterns; uniqueness of base-2 positional representation. Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 2, 4.1 (Positional number systems). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): 2^8 = 256 patterns, 0..255 (sum of 128..1 = 255); unique base-2 representation. Stage message at n = 255 reads 'All 8 on = 255: one less than the next switch, 256. With 0, that is 256 numbers.' (isAllOnesBelowTop branch, also reached via +1 from 254).

claims.text: Switches worth 1, 2, 4, ... always add up to one less than the next switch would be worth.
A ninth switch would be worth 256, one more than all eight together can make.
claims.source: 2^(k+1) = 2 * 2^k: each old pattern appears once with the new switch off and once with it on. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): Ninth switch = 2 x 128 = 256 = 255 + 1. Stage: '255 + 1 = 256 needs a ninth switch'; reveal 'a ninth switch, worth 256'. Housekeeping: source line argues pattern doubling, which is not the claim; the claim follows from doubling place values.

claims.text: A byte is 8 bits; counting with only on and off switches is called binary, and each switch is a bit.
claims.source: Byte = 8 bits (octet) per IEC 80000-13:2008; 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 (arithmetic). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): Byte = 8 bits in current use (IEC 80000-13:2008, byte as synonym of octet; not opened, network blocked); bit = binary digit. Housekeeping (non-blocking): the source line still carries an unused '2^32 = 4,294,967,296' fragment.

claims.text: Adding 1 to 127 flips all eight switches (01111111 becomes 10000000); 255 + 1 = 256 needs a ninth switch, so an 8-switch counter rolls all eight back to 0.
claims.source: 127 = 01111111, 128 = 10000000 differ in all 8 bits; the carry runs through every 1. 255 + 1 = 256 = 2^8 needs a ninth switch, so an 8-switch counter wraps to 0. Flip count (trailing ones + 1) checked for every n in 0..255 in artifacts/scratch/fc2-binary-numbers.mjs. v2 stage messages: '127 + 1 = 128: 8 switches flip, carrying left like 9 + 1 = 10.' and '255 + 1 = 256 needs a ninth switch, so all eight roll back to 0.' Text changed in v2; needs an independent check.

claims.text: Carrying in binary works like carrying in ordinary decimal counting (9 + 1 = 10): when +1 meets a switch that is already on, it turns it off and carries one to the switch on its left.
claims.source: Positional addition with carry is the same procedure in any base (Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 2, 4.1 and 4.3.1). In base 2, 1 + 1 = 10, as 9 + 1 = 10 in base 10. Added v2 for the stage message shown when +1 flips more than one switch.

claims.text: Each switch is worth one more than all the switches to its right put together (for example 128 = 127 + 1), and a computer byte is eight such switches (bits).
claims.source: Restates c3 (2^k = (2^0 + ... + 2^(k-1)) + 1) and c5 (byte = 8 bits, IEC 80000-13). Added v2 for the reveal and the stage message 'All N on = 2^N - 1: one less than the next switch, 2^N'.

recall.question: Ten on/off switches are worth 1, 2, 4, ... up to 512. What is the biggest number they can make?
recall.why: All on is one less than the next switch would be worth: 1,024 - 1 = 1,023.
